title: El Niño, Japan's Ban, and the Iran War: The Perfect Storm Threatening India's 2026 Mango Season
excerpt: As diaspora demand for Indian mangoes hits record levels in America, a triple crisis of weather, geopolitics, and trade disputes is squeezing the supply chain from orchard to Costco shelf.
body:
For millions of Indians abroad, summer is defined by the arrival of mangoes from home. The annual ritual of sourcing Alphonso, Kesar, and Langra varieties — shipped halfway around the world in refrigerated cargo holds — has become a multi-million-dollar seasonal economy. But 2026 is shaping up to be the most challenging mango season in recent memory, as three simultaneous crises converge on India's most culturally significant fruit.

## The Weather: 85 to 90 Percent Crop Losses

In Maharashtra's Alphonso-growing belt — the coastal region around Devgad and Ratnagiri that produces the famed "King of Mangoes" — the damage is staggering. A government-backed survey reviewed by Reuters estimates crop losses of 85 to 90 percent this season.

The culprit is El Niño, the climate pattern that has supercharged temperatures across South Asia. A sharp difference between day and nighttime temperatures during December and January disrupted flowering and fruit setting. Then, unusually intense heat in April and May spoiled the fruit itself.

"If we don't deliver on our orders, the big clients will not return next year," Komal Walke, a 26-year-old horticulturist in Devgad, told Reuters. She has been forced to source Alphonso from larger farms to keep her father's business afloat.

India produces nearly 28 million metric tonnes of mangoes annually — roughly half the world's supply. The domestic market alone was worth $2.3 billion last year. But when the orchards fail, the pain radiates outward.

## The Japan Ban: A 20-Year Trade Corridor Shattered

Compounding the supply crisis, Japan has suspended imports of fresh Indian mangoes for the entire 2026 season — the first major restriction in nearly two decades.

Japanese inspectors discovered deficiencies in fumigation and disinfection practices at Indian treatment facilities during March inspections. The Yokohama Plant Protection Association announced that mango shipments carrying Indian inspection certificates issued after March 25 would no longer be accepted.

Six premium varieties are affected: Alphonso, Kesar, Langra, Banganapalli, Chausa, and Malika. While Japan is not India's largest mango export market — it imported $1.54 million worth in 2025 — the ban carries reputational weight. Exporters fear it could invite increased scrutiny from other import markets.

Regional competitors including Pakistan, Vietnam, Thailand, and Mexico are already positioning themselves to capture Japan's alternative supply.

## The Iran War: Shipping in Crisis

The third blow comes from geopolitics. The ongoing conflict in West Asia has disrupted shipping lanes critical for mango exports. Refrigerated containers — essential for transporting the perishable fruit — have become scarce and expensive. Freight charges have more than doubled, according to exporters.

Shridhar Pathak, co-founder of mango exporter Shreevali Agro, told Reuters that delays and cancellations to consignments for the Gulf, including Dubai and Oman, have cut his shipments by nearly 40 percent. Mangoes originally bound for export are being diverted to domestic markets, paradoxically driving local prices down even as supply shrinks.

## The Diaspora Impact: $50 Boxes and Season Passes

For Indian Americans, the mango season has become serious business. Companies like San Jose-based Shastha Foods have built a devoted following by importing Indian varieties to the West Coast — their "Mangofest" tasting event drew over 1,100 people to a North San Jose warehouse. The Wall Street Journal recently reported that multiple importers are in talks with Costco and Walmart for trial runs, though executives noted that Indian mangoes cost five times the price of regular varieties.

In Seattle, Indian Consul General Prakash Gupta confirmed that Kesar mangoes hit Costco shelves for the first time this season, part of a "mango diplomacy" initiative following a consulate-hosted tasting event.

Chicago-based importer Jaidev Sharma's ZZ Mango now offers a mango season pass — a weekly box for the duration of the season for close to $1,000. Preorders sold out before the first mango left India in April. "Our most loyal customers are Americans," Sharma told the WSJ. "Indian expats tend to complain about the price."

## What's Next

Exporters say talks with Japanese authorities are underway, but the 2026 export season — which runs primarily from April to June — may already be lost for that market. The El Niño-driven crop damage will take at least a year to recover from. And the shipping crisis shows no signs of easing.

For the diaspora, the message is simple: if you can find Indian mangoes this summer, buy them. The supply chain that delivers that $50 box of nostalgia to your doorstep has never been more fragile.
author: Diaspora Desk
